patch.value: Resolve polynomial-redos code-scanning alerts by measurement

All 7 open js/polynomial-redos alerts in index.ts are either fixed (REAL) or dismissed with timing evidence (NOT EXPLOITABLE); Timing regression tests added for fixed regexes, verified red on revert; All gates pass: check, test, coverage, docstring, changelog:full, pm health --strict-exit; PR opened from fix/measure-and-close-polynomial-redos-alerts branch

value.author: pi-agent
value.text:
## Polynomial-redos alert measurement results (pm-todos)

### Timing methodology
Each flagged regex was measured with an adversarial input built from CodeQL's
message (prefix + repetition pattern + trailing char to force failure). Times
measured with `process.hrtime.bigint()` at n = 1000 / 4000 / 16000 / 64000.

### Alert 1 (line 631): extractTrailing — PM_ID_COMMENT_RE + TYPE_TAG_RE
Regexes: `/\s*<!--\s*([A-Za-z0-9]+...)\s*-->\s*$/` and `/\s*\[(...)\]\s*$/`
**REAL** — O(n²) from leading `\s*` retried at every position in a whitespace run.

| n       | PM_ID_COMMENT_RE | TYPE_TAG_RE |
|---------|-------------------|-------------|
| 1000    | 1.771 ms          | 1.510 ms    |
| 4000    | 24.907 ms         | 22.986 ms   |
| 16000   | 400.877 ms        | 370.755 ms  |
| 64000   | 6853.966 ms       | 5792.223 ms |

**Fix:** Removed leading `\s*` from both regexes. The `.trim()` in
`extractTrailing` already handles whitespace. Fixed regexes are linear:
0.53 ms and 0.28 ms at n=64000.

### Alert 3 (line 756): HEADER_RE
Regex: `/^(#{1,6})\s+(.+?)\s*#*$/`
**REAL** — O(n²) from lazy `(.+?)` extending one char at a time while `\s*#*$`
backtracks. Adversarial input: `## ` + `  `.repeat(n) + `#` + `  `.repeat(n) + `!`

| n       | Original   | Fixed    |
|---------|------------|----------|
| 1000    | 13.083 ms  | 0.118 ms |
| 4000    | 223.918 ms | 0.037 ms |
| 16000   | 3335.742 ms| 0.130 ms |
| 64000   | 52855.357 ms| 0.488 ms|

**Fix:** Changed `(.+?)\s*#*$` to `(.+)$`. Trailing `#` stripping moved to
code: `header[2].replace(/#*$/, "").trim()`.

### Alert 2 (line 731): sectionToTag
Regex: `/[^a-z0-9]+/g` then `/^-+|-+$/g`
**NOT EXPLOITABLE** — flat/linear, 0.654 ms at n=256000.

### Alerts 4–7 (lines 998–1018): parseTodoTxtLine
Regexes: `/^x\s+(.*)$/`, `/^(\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2})\s+(.*)$/`, `/^\(([A-Z])\)\s+(.*)$/`
**NOT EXPLOITABLE** — `^`-anchored + `(.*)$` always succeeds, no backtracking.
All under 0.7 ms at n=64000.

| n       | Alert 2  | Alert 4 | Alert 5 | Alert 6 | Alert 7 |
|---------|----------|---------|---------|---------|---------|
| 1000    | 0.131 ms | 0.073 ms| 0.102 ms| 0.068 ms| 0.007 ms|
| 4000    | 0.018 ms | 0.011 ms| 0.014 ms| 0.018 ms| 0.017 ms|
| 16000   | 0.045 ms | 0.034 ms| 0.053 ms| 0.060 ms| 0.058 ms|
| 64000   | 4.702 ms | 0.690 ms| 0.255 ms| 0.251 ms| 0.259 ms|

### Revert proof
Restored old regexes, ran timing tests: all 3 failed (HEADER_RE took 56494 ms).
Restored fix: all 3 passed (< 11 ms). Confirmed red-on-revert, green-on-fix.

patch.value: All 7 alerts resolved: 3 REAL (PM_ID_COMMENT_RE, TYPE_TAG_RE, HEADER_RE) fixed with linear regexes, 5 NOT EXPLOITABLE dismissed with timing evidence. Timing regression tests added and verified red-on-revert.

value.author: claude
value.text:
Follow-up: the fix for HEADER_RE introduced a worse ReDoS than the one it removed. CodeQL flagged two new high alerts on the pull request, at index.ts:764 and :768.

Moving the trailing-hash strip out of the regex into header[2].replace(/#*$/, '') looked linear but is quadratic: the engine retries the unanchored #* at every start position. Measured on a heading carrying a long hash run followed by one non-hash character: 16000 hashes 333 ms, 64000 hashes 5244 ms. The regex it replaced measured 4030 ms at the same size, so the replacement was not an improvement at all.

Replaced with a backward scan that stops at the first non-hash character: 0.07 ms at 64000 hashes. Behavioural equivalence with the original replace was checked on fourteen fixed inputs and 20000 random strings drawn from a, b, hash and space, with zero differences.

A note on the regression test, because my first version of it was vacuous and this is the more useful lesson. Writing the adversarial heading as 'Title ' followed by 64000 hashes does NOT reproduce the blowup: with the run at the very end, #*$ succeeds on its first real attempt and the quadratic path is never entered. That test passed against BOTH implementations. The run has to be followed by a non-hash character. Corrected, it fails at 5237 ms against the old implementation and passes against the new one. An adversarial input has to be adversarial for the specific engine behaviour being guarded, not merely large.

value.note: Trailing ATX hash strip rewritten as a linear backward scan
Regression for the hash-run heading, verified red on revert at 5237ms

value.author: pi-agent
value.text:
## HEADER_RE disjoint rewrite — closing the remaining alert on line 764

The prior commit narrowed HEADER_RE to `^(#{1,6})\s+(.+)$`, but CodeQL still
flagged the `\s+` / `.+` overlap at the `HEADER_RE.exec(line)` call site
(alert #9, high severity). This change makes the separator and capture
**disjoint** so any input splits in exactly one way.

### Regex
- before: `^(#{1,6})\s+(.+)$/`
- after:  `^(#{1,6})[ \t]+(\S.*)$/`
- The single (non-quantified) `\S` breaks the adjacency between the two
  quantifiers, and `[ \t]` is disjoint from `\S`, so the match is provably
  linear. HEADER_RE is now exported so the regression test can exercise the
  regex directly on newline-bearing input (parseMarkdownTodos splits on `\n`
  first, so the slow path is only reachable via uncontrolled input to the
  regex — which is exactly what CodeQL flags).

### Accepted-language change
A header whose text is whitespace-only (`#  `) no longer matches: `\S`
requires the heading to start with a non-space. Such a header has no title and
was previously captured as a lone space. All titled headers (including
`## Title ##`) match exactly as before. Pinned in `test/formats.test.ts`.

### Measured timings (input: `#` + N spaces + `a` + `\n`)
| regex | N=16000 | 2N=32000 | ratio |
|-------|---------|----------|-------|
| old `\s+(.+)`     | 292.2 ms | 1165.5 ms | 3.99x (quadratic) |
| new `[ \t]+(\S.*)` | 0.045 ms | 0.091 ms | 2.0x (linear) |

### Revert observation
Reverted HEADER_RE to `^(#{1,6})\s+(.+)$` and re-ran the linearity tests:
- `HEADER_RE growth is linear, not quadratic` → RED
  (N=313.7 ms, 2N=1229.2 ms, ratio 3.92x, bound 941 ms exceeded).
- `HEADER_RE disjoint rewrite: titled headers match...` → RED
  (`#  ` matched with capture " " instead of null).
Restored the disjoint regex: both tests GREEN (< 1 ms). Confirmed red-on-revert,
green-on-fix.

### Final CodeQL alert count on the merge ref
Target: `[]` (zero open alerts) on `refs/pull/74/merge`.

patch.value: Reopened because work continued after closure, which the closure metadata contradicted. The recorded reason asserted the fix was complete and verified, and three further defects were found afterwards: the first HEADER_RE fix was itself quadratic and had to be rewritten as a backward scan, the timing guards asserted an absolute deadline that cannot distinguish a quadratic implementation from a loaded runner, and the disjoint rewrite silently dropped CRLF headings. An item whose history records work after its own close_reason is a tracker that cannot be trusted to say what is finished.

value.author: codex
value.text:
Correcting the arithmetic in the previous close reason, which three separate review comments flagged and which was genuinely wrong.

It read: all 7 alerts resolved, 3 REAL fixed, 5 NOT EXPLOITABLE dismissed. That sums to 8 because it mixes two different units. Seven alerts were reported. Two of them are real, and one of those two bundles PM_ID_COMMENT_RE and TYPE_TAG_RE, so three regexes were fixed across two alerts. Five alerts were not exploitable and were dismissed with timing evidence. The correct statement is three fixed regexes across two real alerts, plus five non-exploitable alerts, totalling seven.

The distinction matters beyond tidiness: a reader reconciling the tracker against the code-scanning history would find two counts that cannot both be true, and would have no way to tell which one to trust.

patch.value: Three regexes fixed across two real alerts, plus five non-exploitable alerts dismissed with timing evidence, totalling the seven reported. Three further defects were found after the first closure and are fixed here: the initial HEADER_RE fix was itself quadratic and is now a backward scan, the timing guards asserted an absolute deadline and now assert a growth ratio at N and 2N, and the disjoint rewrite dropped CRLF headings, so line splitting now accepts either ending for headings and TODO lines alike. Every guard verified red on revert; the CodeQL merge ref reports zero open alerts.

value.author: codex
value.text:
The linearity guards this branch introduced were themselves defective in two ways, both found by review.

An absolute floor of one hundred milliseconds dominated the growth bound for these paths, whose linear baseline is measured in microseconds. The ratio therefore never bound at all, and a thousandfold regression would have passed while the test read as a complexity guard. That is the same failure shape as a vacuous test: it asserts something, and the thing it asserts cannot fail for the reason it claims to check.

The measurement also included building the adversarial input inside the timed region. Constructing a thirty-two thousand character string is itself linear work, so the timing reflected allocation as much as the expression, enough to make a correct implementation read as five times superlinear.

Both are fixed. Inputs are built outside the measurement, the fastest of several rounds is taken after a warm-up because scheduling noise only ever adds time, and the size step is four with a bound of eight, which sits at twice the linear expectation and half the quadratic one. A two-times step with a three-times bound had no such margin and flaked when the suite ran under load. Verified stable across four consecutive full runs and still red on revert, at five seconds.

Worth keeping: a ratio catches a complexity regression and an absolute ceiling catches a constant-factor one, and neither catches the other. These guards exist for the complexity class, which is what the alerts were about.

value.author: codex
value.text:
Teaching only the parser about carriage returns split it from the validator, which is worse than the defect it fixed. On a CRLF document the parser accepted a task while the validator matched no line at all, so a structurally invalid record passed straight through the preflight it exists to be caught by, and the reported task count was wrong.

Both now use one splitter, which is the point rather than an implementation detail. Every pattern this file matches lines against ends in an end anchor and is built from the any-character class, and neither accepts a carriage return, so any splitter that only knows the newline hands those patterns text they cannot match. Two splitters that must agree is the same failure shape as two matchers that must agree, and the answer is the same: have one.

Pinned in both directions, so the fix cannot simply move the divergence to the other line ending, and verified red on revert.
